Samantha, Diego —

Thanks — attached is a first-pass implementation matrix (implementation-matrix-v1.xlsx) and a small SDK stub bundle (sdk-stubs.zip) with examples in Swift, Kotlin, and Node. Key points up-front:

1) Sandbox -> Prod mapping and endpoint migration
- Sandbox host: https://sandbox.api.redwood.ai/v1 -> Prod host: https://api.redwood.ai/v1
- For dedicated/private customers we provide a custom base URL; your current Hosted plan will use the public host above.

2) Token & auth recommendations
- Use short-lived tokens (15–60m) with silent refresh.
- Mobile: store refresh tokens in OS-kept secure storage (iOS Keychain / Android Keystore).

3) Retries & timeouts (mobile-first defaults)
- Connect timeout: 3s
- Read timeout: 10s
- Retry policy: client-side idempotent request retry for 429/5xx only, up to 3 attempts with full-jitter exponential backoff (base 250ms, max 2000ms).
- For streaming/generation endpoints use long-poll heartbeat instead of aggressive retries.

4) Rate limit handling
- Server returns X-RateLimit-Remaining / Retry-After headers. Respect Retry-After before retrying.
- Implement token-level in-memory counters (per device) for burst smoothing.

5) Endpoint cutover pattern (recommended)
- Phase 1: Shadow traffic for 48–72h to new endpoint (responses ignored by client)
- Phase 2: Canary rollout (1–5% of users) for 24–48h with monitoring on latency/error budget
- Phase 3: Gradual ramp to 100% with abort criteria (error rate spike > 1.5x baseline OR tail latency > 2x).

6) Fallbacks and graceful degradation
- If primary generation fails, fallback to a smaller/faster variant (e.g., redwood-small) and surface a degraded UX banner.

Attached sample Node snippet (from sdk-stubs.zip):

// Node example: simple retry wrapper
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
async function callWithRetries(url, opts, attempts = 3) {
  let attempt = 0;
  while (attempt < attempts) {
    try {
      const resp = await fetch(url, opts);
      if (resp.status === 429 || resp.status >= 500) {
        const retryAfter = resp.headers.get('retry-after');
        if (retryAfter) await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, parseInt(retryAfter) * 1000));
        throw new Error('retryable');
      }
      return resp;
    } catch (err) {
      attempt++;
      if (attempt >= attempts) throw err;
      const backoff = Math.min(2000, 250 * Math.pow(2, attempt)) * (0.5 + Math.random() / 2);
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, backoff));
    }
  }
}

Diego —

Answers inline:

1) Mid-flight token revocation
- If a token is revoked mid-flight the request will fail with 401. Our guidance: implement an immediate token refresh + one retry. To avoid cascades we recommend a 60s grace window where refreshes are accepted on the old token server-side while revocation metadata propagates. We'll document this and add the sequence diagram to implementation-matrix-v1.xlsx.

2) SSO / IdP changes
- No special headers required; Redwood accepts standard bearer tokens in Authorization: Bearer <token>. For enterprises we support introspection endpoints and custom header passthrough if you plan to use opaque tokens — we'll coordinate with your IdP team.

3) Rate limit headers
- Hosted API: returns X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset (epoch seconds), and a Retry-After (seconds) on 429 responses. There are no burst tokens returned in headers; burst allowances are enforced server-side.
